Furthermore, the intention here is that one who has severed distinct delusions enters the stages and abidings; such a person is not one who is driven by others.

Furthermore, although this [palace] and the one in the intermediate state are both equally the retributive enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogika-vipāka*), since this [palace] demonstrates entry into the realm of Akṣobhya as the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and the beginning of all teachings, it is augmented with a white whisk made of *rajas-kīrṇa* (dust-destroying) silk and covered by a precious canopy of compassion.
The preceding section described what the elder possessed; this section clarifies what the impoverished son perceives.
Since what they possess is identical, the detailed and abbreviated versions are applied interchangeably.

Regarding the phrase "standing in attendance" followed by "and so forth": since this constitutes the skillful means of the Middle Way, it is appropriate to interpret the officials and commoners as being prior to the [ten] stages (bhūmi). This is because the central figure, the two attendants, and the populace differ. One should clarify, according to the respective sections, the sequential and non-sequential aspects, even down to the differences between the teachers of the two teachings, each of whom has distinct characteristics regarding standing in attendance and fanning away dust.

Regarding "hanging various flower banners": the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) manifesting supernatural powers for the benefit of those below is what is meant by "hanging. Although both flowers and banners hang down, the flowers adorn the banners; it is like when one sees the four means of integration being manifested, the observer gives rise to joy.
Furthermore, although both the banners and the flowers move, their designations differ: the banners signify turning and revolving, while the flowers signify elegance and beauty.

When supernatural powers descend to transform beings and cause them to rejoice, these two elements are employed to ensure they reach the highest level of the unconditioned (*anālambana*). Therefore, they are suspended together upon the canopy to accord with the essence [of the Buddha], as if completely covering him above.

Regarding the phrase "fragrant water" and so forth: if one follows the second interpretation concerning one's own practice, if fragrant water were not sprinkled upon the ground, then the canopies, banners, and flowers would be defiled by dust. Therefore, by sprinkling the ground of the true mark (*dharmatā*) with the fragrant water of wisdom, one removes the dust of the three delusions; thus, the Tathāgata—the elder—and [his virtues such as] compassion and the rest become equally pure.

If one follows the first interpretation, which explains that scented water is sprinkled upon the Bodhisattva’s "mind-ground," since this is explained as arising from the cultivation of causes for the benefit of others, one should know that the seven purities must likewise be explained as arising from the causal practices of a Bodhisattva.

Although the names are the same as those in the Lesser Vehicle, this is in fact the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); therefore, the Three Collections (*tripiṭaka*) and the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and others are cited.

If one were to rely on the provisional [teachings], the meanings would differ according to the instructions; however, here we rely on the Perfect Mind, wherein all things are distributed across the various stages (*bhūmi*) by means of these seven [categories]. One practices these oneself and causes others to cultivate them; for this reason, the commentary throughout relies entirely on the Perfect interpretation.

Regarding the phrase "arrayed" and so forth: the flowers symbolize the adornment of the cause, while the jewels symbolize the virtues of the fruit. Since the myriad virtues of both cause and fruit all adorn the ultimate reality, they are thus arranged and spread across the ground.
The ground is not made of flower-jewels, yet flower-jewels are arrayed upon it; principle is not cause and effect, yet one cultivates and realizes cause and effect.

Regarding the phrase "the taking out and putting in are as explained previously, etc.," this refers to the preceding four stages; however, while those [stages] pertain solely to the fruit, these may also pertain to the cause.

Regarding "Ocean of Marks" (xiānghǎi), this refers entirely to the "Chapter on the Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Marks" (*Rúlái xiānghǎi pǐn*) and the "Chapter on the Radiance of the Minor Marks" (*Suíhǎo guānmíng pǐn*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. These chapters clarify that Vairocana is endowed with as many marks as there are atoms in ten lotus-flower treasury world-oceans (*padmakośa-lokadhātu-samudra*), each of which is adorned with exquisite features; therefore, it says, "One must explain it by way of Śākyamuni."

Regarding the phrase "The four [beings] see their father and flee in fear": although the mutual encounter between father and son is an inconceivable manifestation of the resonance between the Way and its response, when discussed in terms of the gradual teaching within the events of transformation, it is according to principle that if one says the father sees the son first, it signifies the Tathāgata’s discernment of the [son's] capacity.

The current statement that "the son first saw the father's appearance and his dwelling place" and so forth does not mean he had already seen them; rather, these are all spoken in accordance with the capacities of the audience. One should fully recount the beginning and end, as well as the original causes for his transformation through the teachings.

Regarding the phrase "or kings, or those like kings," since it says they saw their father and feared to avoid him, this refers to the very beginning of the sudden and gradual teachings. If one considers the period prior to these teachings, there was as yet no concern regarding the fear of Māra; thus, in relation to the gradual-capacity practitioners who feared and avoided [the Great Treatise], it is said, "never before seen or heard," and so forth.

From the section "Brief Opening" (*lue kai*) onwards, the preceding is verified; it can be verified that in the past, at the very beginning, he committed a greater fault than Śāriputra when hearing the brief exposition, and thus it is said, "he has a fault even greater than today."

Furthermore, the meaning of the subsequent section is to re-explain that those of limited capacity could not have known of the two bodies at that time; thus, this describes how they did not receive [the teaching] among their own capacities, just as a destitute son might see a king or his like.
Question:
The Dharma is the teacher, yet the roles of teacher and disciple are distinct; how can they be considered equal? Answer:
"This is the son of the Equal Teacher; his realization accords with the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "All sutras are called 'Kings of Sutras,'" this is a further explanation based on the teaching: among all sutras, those that clarify the meaning of the Dharmakāya are designated as Kings of Sutras.

Because wisdom accords with the Dharma and is commensurate with names and so forth, within the context of the capacities of sentient beings, the Dharma is contrasted with wisdom, and they are designated as "king" and "king-like," respectively. This refers to the relationship between the various Mahāyāna schools and the Hīnayāna. Worldly people do not understand this; seeing that all Mahāyāna teachings are called "kings of sūtras," they claim that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is equal to other teachings.

Now, it is said that both "milk" and the two types of "ghee" refer to the Dharma-body and the Reward-body; although both are called "kings," they are not the "Kings of all Sutras. Even if a sutra were to say "the king of all sutras," it would not say "that which I shall now speak is the foremost"; furthermore, its meaning can be understood through the context of what is being contrasted.
"Si" (肆) means to release, to discharge, or to extend. Regarding the subsequent analogy of the father seeing his son under "Shifu" (時富):

while the śrāvakas were like the son who saw the father in the previous analogy, they skillfully grasped the small [teaching] but encountered the great [truth] and their faculties were such that they could not receive it; now, by establishing the analogy of the father seeing the son, there is a subtle metaphor for the Buddha perceiving the capacities of beings, which he understands thoroughly without needing to deliberate.

Regarding the phrase "seeing the child's location," the Tathāgata does not experience joy or the fulfillment of his vows upon arising from an empty seat; therefore, this is merely stated in terms of the pedagogical ritual as "the father seeing the child. How could it be that the Buddha-eye must necessarily wait for the child to see before the father sees?
Regarding the phrase "Now the occasion has come to praise [the Buddha's] compassion," both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are entitled to be called "coming to praise.
The passage beginning with "He clearly extracts suffering" and so forth refers to the *Upamā-parivarta* (The Chapter on Similes).

One should also say that the preceding analogy illustrates how the Tathāgata removes their suffering through compassion; this analogy illustrates how the sons receive the bliss bestowed by the Buddha. Since the Tathāgata’s extraction of suffering fundamentally lies in the bestowal of bliss, once the sons receive the bliss, they already know that their suffering has been extracted. Thus, the meaning in both instances is identical, though they appear alternately according to the specific passage.

Regarding the passage from "He then had this thought" to "could not [attain it]," this also describes the period following his regression from the Mahāyāna. Having entered the five sensory objects, he found that the Great Dharma was no longer effective for him; he then sought out minor methods, which eventually became applicable as his faculties gradually matured, at which point he finally employed the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle.

Regarding the statement "taking the small," this does not mean that [the recipient] had already attained the small in the past, nor does it refer to the initial smallness at the beginning of the present life. Therefore, since in former days there was no designation of a "capacity" (根機) for the teaching to arrive, nor any discussion of the entrustment of the treasure, and because there was no joy [at that time], it is simply said: "In the past, seeing [him], I wished to give [it]," and so forth.

Regarding the passage from "Today" to "there is something to be entrusted": seeing that those of small capacity have reached the point where they know the Great [Teaching] is not far off, he therefore rejoices that they are grounds for the entrustment of the treasure.

The phrase "I always" below explains that following the previous discussion on the regression from the Mahāyāna and prior to the sudden and gradual teachings, there was never a time when he did not contemplate both the Great and Small vehicles.
Although both have been lost, because his circulation [in the world] is contrasted with his compassion, it is for this reason that the entrustment of the Dharma-treasure exists at this present time.
Regarding the phrase, "Now there are sentient beings with the capacity for deliverance," and so forth: Question:
Since sentient beings with the capacity [for deliverance] arise by means of the Buddha, why is it said that they come of their own accord? Answer:

Although the arising of the capacity (indriya) depends on the Buddha, its manifestation also depends on the sentient being. For now, let us consider this by way of a worldly elder lamenting that his son has come of his own accord; while previously the capacity had not arisen, it is hoped that it may now be awakened. Thus, one should lament that the capacity has been awakened and call it "coming of one's own accord."
If the capacity for response has not yet arisen and the pursuit has still not arrived, how could it come of its own accord?

The phrase "Although I... below explores the discourse on the later period; perhaps because there is no further entrustment to repay [the debt] of this single period, one cherishes it. Just as when chanting the Dharma of *parinirvāṇa*, all things follow toward extinction and are on the verge of extinction, yet they are still cherished; therefore, it is called "although" (*sui*).

Regarding the phrase "immediately dispatching others," and so forth: since from this point onward the teaching of sudden and gradual transformation is taken up, we know that what precedes it represents the sudden and gradual [teachings] prior to this, whether great or small.
Regarding the passage from "Only the 'Expedient Means' Chapter" to "and including the leading," the intended meaning is as follows:
although the text may vary in length, the underlying intent must remain the same. Since the "Expedient Means" is intended for those of superior faculties, it does not require a separate exposition;
since the parables are intended for those of middling capacity, they must be extracted from the general discourse to present them separately.

Although the *Sūtra* and its verses are somewhat abbreviated, they take the parable as primary while the other elements are mutually integrated; since we have now grasped the parable, it is necessary to describe them all in full.

Regarding the statement, “Only in the ‘Expedient Means’ chapter is there a general admonition and exhortation,” etc., fearing that the seeker might become confused, I shall again provide a detailed commentary. In the section on Śākyamuni within the text of the ‘Expedient Means’ chapter, it simply says, “He set aside the Great [Vehicle] and bestowed the Small [Vehicle]. Although it does not explicitly distinguish between admonition and exhortation, the underlying intent of the words lies in exhortation; thus, the passage beginning with “During the twenty-one days he contemplated such matters” refers precisely to the Great [Vehicle].
"The dull faculties of sentient beings" refers to their lack of spiritual capacity (*amūka*).
"Beings such as these" refers to the cessation of transformative teaching (*śānta-vinaya*).
"He immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī," and so forth, refers to the bestowal of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Although the term "admonition" (jiei) is not explicitly mentioned, its meaning encompasses two gates.
Regarding the phrase "the burning house opens the exhortation and admonition to depart": thus, from the Dharma-exposition (hosetsu), there is the opening of the exhortation and the admonition.
Regarding the phrase "explaining each as three": within the gate of exhortation, there are three [sections].
The initial passage, "The elder had this thought," and so forth, is intended as an appropriate proposal;
the subsequent passage, "He further reflected upon this house," and so forth, indicates that there was no receptive capacity [in the listeners].
The phrase "or they shall fall" and so forth refers to relinquishment.
Regarding the three aspects of the gate of admonition: first, the statement "I shall preach for them" and so forth refers to the preliminary suitability.
"Although his father felt compassion," and so forth, refers to the lack of spiritual capacity (*agotra*).
"Running back and forth to the east and west," and so forth, refers to being abandoned.
Regarding the statement, "In the long prose, there is exhortation but no admonition," there are three types of exhortation:
The initial passage, "The Tathāgata further had this thought: 'If I were to merely... and so forth, refers to what is appropriate [for the teaching].
The subsequent passage, "For what reason?
Because these sentient beings have not yet escaped... and so forth, refers to what they do not accept.
The passage beginning with "Just as that householder, although... and so forth refers to the cessation of the transformative teaching (*śāsanopasaṃhāra*).

Regarding the statement "the text on the cessation of the transformative teaching is extensive," it first cites the three preceding parables and subsequently applies those three to the actual subject matter to clearly elucidate the cessation of the transformative teaching.
The first part is like that elder: the initial section, which does not provide even a single analogy, serves to pacify and transform [the listeners] by directly applying [the teaching].

Next, from "But with earnestness" onwards, it applies the bestowal of the small [vehicle]; from "Then each was given" onwards, it applies the equal distribution; these two sides together serve to pacify and transform.
Next, the sixteen characters beginning with "The Tathāgata likewise... mark the true commencement of the cessation of transformation; therefore, it is called "extensive.
Regarding the phrase "In the verse, however, only the admonitions [are given]," this also comprises three parts:
first, the four and a half lines beginning with "It is appropriate to provide rescue and relief" constitute the section on the provisional suitability (*nīya*).
Next, the three lines beginning with "The sons were ignorant" eulogize their refusal [to accept the carts].
The single line "in play" eulogizes the cessation of the transformation.
The following belongs to the section on the use of the carts.

This verse consists of three parts in its metaphorical section; however, in the corresponding application (*yōjā*), it likewise only applies the admonition. There is one line of extended verse that admits two interpretations, both of which possess the three parts. The first interpretation is as follows: the phrase "although he instructs and exhorts" represents the suitability [of the teaching]; the phrase "yet they do not believe or accept it" indicates the lack of capacity (*mūka*); and the two phrases "regarding various desires and defilements" signify the cessation of the transformative activity.

Furthermore, it is said that the final two lines following "Alternatively" (*huò kě*) also eulogize the absence of receptive capacity (*wú jī*), because they rely on the second interpretation; thus it is stated that "they do not eulogize the cessation of transformation.
The passage beginning with "He immediately dispatched an attendant" serves to present the collective summary.
However, while there are six meanings, there are only five textual sections:
first, the exhortations and admonitions each have two parts, namely "appropriateness" and "lack of capacity";
next, the exhortations and admonitions are combined into one, which refers to the cessation of the transformative teaching through the two gates.
The Record of the Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Seven, Part One.
